parsing_res_list.block_content: In this section, we have shown that our implementation of Veritas (Kafka) can achieve close to 30,000 TPS with a block size of 100 and close to 65,000 TPS with a block size of 1,000 transactions, both with sub-second latency. On the other hand, the systems using Tendermint have low throughput, of up to 1,750 TPS, and high latency of up to 2 seconds. Our implementation of Veritas (TM) exhibits higher throughput than BigchainDB and BigchainDB (PV). This is because BigchainDB has a complex and redundant transaction validation mechanism which slows down the entire system. BlockchainDB has a throughput of less than 100 TPS because it uses Ethereum as its underlying storage engine. In summary, CFT systems, which are closer to the design of distributed databases, achieve higher performance compared to the systems based on BFT consensus but do not offer protection in Byzantine environments.

In this section, we discuss some trade-offs that users and developers need to consider when using and designing a hybrid blockchain database system. We look at these trade-offs from the perspective of performance, security, and ease of development.

CFT vs. BFT. Adopting a CFT or BFT consensus protocol depends on the environment where the system is supposed to operate. Nonetheless, it is well-known that BFT consensus is much slower than CFT consensus [11, 36]. In this paper, we show that the gap between the CFT and BFT systems throughput is 5 – 500×. We also show that the performance of both CFT and BFT systems degrades under poor real-world networking conditions. While typical blockchains employ BFT consensus protocols due to their security guarantees in a Byzantine environment, some permissioned blockchains such as Hyperledger Fabric [18] and R3 Corda [22] are employing CFT consensus protocols, while delegating the security aspects to the blockchain access/membership layer.

When choosing BFT, the main focus of a developer is on optimizing the performance since the security guarantees are relatively high. Query optimization and using high-performance underlying storage are the common methods of optimizing such systems. Optimizing the performance of the BFT consensus is an important aspect that is studied in recent works [3, 29, 46]. In contrast, CFT protocols usually provide high performance and developers need to add verifiable components to provide security guarantees such as building an append-only ledger to provide verifiability.

In summary, CFT hybrid blockchain database systems should be used when there is a demand for high performance without strict security guarantees, such as in online transaction processing (OLTP) systems. When starting with an existing CFT system, the developer can add blockchain features, such as an append-only ledger, to improve security. BFT hybrid blockchain database systems should be used when there is a need for high security, such as for digital assets storage. When starting with an existing BFT system, the developer can add database features, such as parallel validation and query optimization, to improve the performance.

SQL vs. NoSQL. When designing a hybrid blockchain database system, the developer needs to consider the data access model from both the user-level API and underlying storage perspectives. For example, the relational model and its de facto query language, SQL, are widely used in the industry. But adding an SQL API in a hybrid blockchain database system is tedious because we need a layer to parse the SQL statements to basic operations and an optimized execution plan to get higher performance. BRD [31] uses this approach to support SQL. Another option is to add SQL support only to the underlying database, while the SQL queries are forwarded to this database. For example, FalconDB [33] and ChainifyDB [38] use MySQL to provide such a relational model in the underlying database.

On the other hand, many Internet-scale systems use simpler data models, such as key-value stores. For example, NoSQL databases support simpler data models while offering flexibility and scalability. However, they do not offer ACID properties. In this paper, we analyze Veritas and BigchainDB, two systems that rely on NoSQL systems. However, we show that the underlying database, being it NoSQL Redis or SQL RediSQL, has little impact on the performance of Veritas (Kafka) and Veritas (TM).

Using SQL or NoSQL is a trade-off between integrity and flexibility. In SQL, the user must define the table and field structures before adding data. For example, the primary key, index, trigger, and stored procedure of the table must be defined to provide data constraints and prevent the database from storing invalid data. The table structure can be updated after being defined, but this is complicated if there are major structural changes. In NoSQL, data can be added at any time and anywhere, without the need to define the tables first. This provides more flexibility but may result in storing invalid data. In addition, SQL allows the integrity of the database to be constrained by defining foreign keys while there are no options for data integrity constraints in NoSQL.

In this paper, we survey the existing hybrid blockchain database systems proposed by the database community in the last few years. We then conduct a detailed performance analysis of five implementations of hybrid blockchain database systems based on Veritas [19], BlockchainDB [16], and BigchainDB [20]. Our flexible implementation of Veritas allows us to change the key components of the system, such as the consensus middleware and the underlying database, in order to analyze their effect on performance. For example, we replace the CFT Apache Kafka middleware with the BFT Tendermint and observe that the performance drops by more than 15x. However, Tendermint offers security guarantees in a Byzantine environment. On the other hand, we replace the underlying Redis database with RediSQL and MongoDB and observe moderate performance differences. This, together with a breakdown of the time spent in each major component of a hybrid blockchain database system, shows that the consensus protocols are the source of poor performance in these systems.
